title: Strategy Is Choice
coreMove: Recognize that a strategy only exists when its five choices cohere and reinforce each other — a list of ambitions, however detailed, is not a strategy.
sourcePressure: The chapter establishes the book's master frame: strategy is not a vision statement, a plan, or an optimization of the current business. It exists only when a cascade of five integrated choices — winning aspiration, where to play, how to win, capabilities, management systems — each reinforces the others. The Olay turnaround is the anchor: P&G did not rescue the brand by being more energetic; it made a tighter, coherent set of choices that fit together.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: Strategy means having a clear vision and a detailed plan — the more thorough the planning document, the more rigorous the strategy.

sourceAnchors.name: Olay's recovery
sourceAnchors.detail: P&G chose reinvention for Olay rather than incremental maintenance — combining a renamed brand, a clearer target customer, a sharper price-positioning logic, and a choice to compete in a more attractive part of the market. The integrated choices created a coherent way to win.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Olay did not turn around because P&G invested harder in what Olay already was. It turned around because the choices about who the customer was, where the brand would sit in the market, and what the offer would do all pointed in the same direction at once.

hook: Every team thinks they have a strategy — opening that generalizes about 'most companies'
Strategy is simple: just make better decisions — generic coaching opener
counterintuition: The more choices you make, the less strategic flexibility you have — generic trade-off framing
Ambition is not enough without execution — execution-first framing
tryThisNow: Write down your three most important priorities — generic goal-setting prompt
Ask yourself whether your team is aligned on the mission — generic alignment check
examples: A leader writes a new mission statement and calls it strategy
A team holds a strategy day and produces a long slide deck

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: Avoid the shell of timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision repeated across all six slots

exampleSpecs.domain: artisan bakery deciding between wholesale accounts and a direct-to-consumer subscription model
exampleSpecs.audience: a small-business owner who has written down three growth goals but cannot decide which way to invest
exampleSpecs.stakes: investing in the wrong channel depletes cash before the busy season and leaves both paths half-built
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the owner lists the three growth goals — more wholesale accounts, a subscription box, a second location — then realizes that each goal requires a different capability and customer relationship, and the three cannot be pursued at once without none of them cohering
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a whiteboard covered in growth ideas, every one of them plausible, none of them connected
mustInclude: a specific resource constraint that forces the choice
the moment the protagonist sees the three goals pulling in different directions
mustAvoid: advice to hire more staff as the solution

exampleSpecs.domain: a nonprofit choosing between expanding grant-funded program breadth and deepening a single program's outcomes
exampleSpecs.audience: an executive director facing a board that wants growth and funders who want depth
exampleSpecs.stakes: if the org tries to grow program count and deepen impact at the same time, neither goal will be achieved and the largest funder may walk
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the director sees that every program added in the last two years was chased because of a grant opportunity, not because it fit the org's stated aspiration — the wish list grew while the actual strategy dissolved
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a program list that has doubled in three years, each line with a different funder's logo beside it
mustInclude: the gap between the stated mission and the actual portfolio
a moment where the director recognizes that choices were reactive, not strategic
mustAvoid: board conflict drama as the main tension

exampleSpecs.domain: a management consulting practice choosing which client industries to serve
exampleSpecs.audience: a partner-level consultant who wants to grow revenue but has taken on projects in six different sectors
exampleSpecs.stakes: the practice cannot build a repeatable capability in any sector if it keeps dispersing into new ones
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the consultant lays out a pipeline of six potential new engagements in six different industries and recognizes that every proposal requires a different credential they don't have — the cascade question forces a choice about which field to own
exampleSpecs.firstImage: six new proposals on a shared drive, each one in a different sector, none building on the last
mustInclude: the specific cost of re-entering a new sector for each proposal
the realization that the practice has a pipeline but not a strategy
mustAvoid: generic work-life balance or burnout framing
advice to simply say no to clients

exampleSpecs.domain: a community radio station choosing between a hyper-local news format and a broad music and talk format
exampleSpecs.audience: a board and programming director deciding where the station's scarce production capacity should go
exampleSpecs.stakes: the station's current format serves no audience especially well, and digital competitors have already taken the casual listener
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the programming director asks the board which listeners they are actually trying to serve and what beating a podcast would require — the question exposes that the current format was inherited, not chosen, and that no capabilities support either potential direction
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a programming schedule that is half local news, half music, and full of unfilled sponsor slots
mustInclude: the inherited format that nobody chose deliberately
the capability gap that appears when the winning aspiration is named explicitly

exampleSpecs.domain: an academic department deciding whether to compete for graduate student rankings or deepen undergraduate teaching quality
exampleSpecs.audience: a department chair who has received budget for a new hire and must decide what kind of position to fill
exampleSpecs.stakes: the hire will either reinforce a research identity that attracts PhD students or a teaching identity that attracts strong undergraduates — the two paths require different capabilities and different measures of success
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: before: the chair writes a job description that tries to attract a researcher and a teacher at once; after: the chair realizes the description would produce a mediocre outcome in both directions and must choose which aspiration the department is actually pursuing
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a draft job posting that lists twelve criteria, the first six pointing toward research and the last six toward teaching
mustInclude: the specific capability each path requires that the other does not
the moment the chair sees that the job description is a symptom of a missing strategic choice
mustAvoid: academic politics as the main obstacle

exampleSpecs.domain: a regional hardware retailer deciding whether to compete on product selection breadth or on contractor-service relationships
exampleSpecs.audience: a second-generation owner whose store has been caught between a big-box home-improvement chain and a specialty supplier
exampleSpecs.stakes: the store cannot match the big-box on price and selection, and cannot match the specialist on depth — the current position wins on nothing
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the owner traces the last three years of inventory decisions and realizes each one was reactive to a competitor move rather than advancing a coherent identity — the store stocked a bit of everything and won exactly the customers nobody else wanted
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a back storeroom with twelve pallets of slow-moving inventory, each one bought to match a competitor's promotion
mustInclude: the specific customer group the store could actually serve with a different capability
the clear cost of trying to compete in multiple directions at once

skillTargets: distinguish a genuine strategy cascade from a list of ambitions or priorities
apply the coherence test to a specific set of choices to identify misalignment
analyze a real scenario to determine which of the five choices is missing or weak
evaluate whether a plan actually forces a choice or just documents an intention

tryThisNowSpec: Write down the three biggest priorities you are currently pursuing. For each one, ask: does the second priority require a different customer, field, or capability than the first? If yes, name the specific conflict — that gap is where strategy is missing.

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm — a direct second-person challenge, a brief Olay reference grounded in the principle rather than narrative, or a question that puts the reader in the protagonist's seat
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'
